title: Buffered I/O
concept: Buffered I/O improves performance by reducing system calls, but you must understand flush timing

steps.title: Including stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
**`#include <stdio.h>`** -- Header for standard I/O functions like `printf` and `fflush`.

In this lesson we learn about **Buffering**.

steps.title: Starting main function
steps.explanation:
**`int main() {`** -- When the program starts, the OS opens the standard streams and sets a **buffering mode** for each.

C has 3 buffering modes.

steps.title: Storing data in the buffer
steps.explanation:
**`printf("Example 1... ");`** -- `printf` is called but the string ends without **`\n`**.

The data is currently in the `stdout` internal buffer in memory.

steps.title: Forcing buffer flush (Flush)
steps.explanation: **`fflush(stdout);`** -- **Forcefully empties** the specified stream's buffer, immediately sending all accumulated data to its destination. At this point, the buffered `"Example 1... "` is sent to the terminal.

steps.title: Output with newline character
steps.explanation:
**`printf("Printed immediately!
");`** -- This `printf` includes **`
`** at the end. In line buffering, encountering `
` **automatically flushes** the buffer, so it appears on screen immediately without `fflush`.

steps.title: Confirming auto-flush
steps.explanation: **`printf("Example 2 with newline\n");`** -- Since `\n` is included, line buffering automatically flushes and the output appears on screen immediately.
steps.stdout:
Example 1... Printed immediately!
Example 2 with newline

steps.title: Program termination
steps.explanation: **`return 0;`** -- On normal termination, the C runtime automatically flushes all open stream buffers. Even data printed with `printf` without a trailing `\n` gets output at this point.

quiz.question: Why might printf output not appear on screen when a program crashes?
options: The output buffer was not flushed before the process died
quiz.explanation:
If data is only in the buffer (no newline or fflush) when a crash occurs, that data never reaches the screen and is lost.
Be careful when debugging.

misconceptions.correct: Buffering is almost always involved to reduce disk I/O and system call costs (Full, Line, No buffering).

keyTakeaway: Buffering improves performance, but when real-time output is needed or during debugging, understanding fflush is crucial.
